summary: BG2 episode on China's open-source AI lead, the compute arms race and AI funding/pricing, then tariffs. Gerstner argues the Bessent tariff path (about $300B) is working, markets are at highs, and a big China deal is coming.

coverage.note: tariff deals (EU, Japan), intro, guest, AI summit and crypto policy
US regulation, China open-source dominance, compounding and distillation
reasoning models with tools; China open source history
Chinese co-evolution, farmers analogy, AI Action Plan open source
price-performance of Chinese models, US open-source prediction, commoditization
US open-source entrants, brand and liability, OpenAI open model
Meta, values vs price, Chinese release speed, xAI open source
compute arms race, token growth, funding rounds
private vs public risk appetite, capex split, token demand
pricing below cost, price curve, cost optimization, open-source use by coding agents

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Everybody said this was going to lead to retaliation to trade wars was going to be disastrous for the US and all we've seen so far is deals deals deals deals.
claims.claim: US tariff threats produced trade deals (EU 15% in, 0% out plus $750B energy purchases; Japan $550B investment) rather than retaliation, so consensus fears of trade war were too pessimistic.
claims.testable: partly - outcome observed over one half-year

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: excess regulation on everything from energy production to model development to semiconductor chip distribution.
claims.claim: Excess US regulation of energy, model development and chip distribution was an unforced error that gave China momentum in AI.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: they're dominating the global landscape for open-source models.
claims.claim: China leads global open-source AI models (six to seven high-quality providers; Qwen over 400M downloads) while Llama 4 is sputtering.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: they're able to compound. So what you're seeing very quickly is both the open- source nature, the open weights nature, uh, allow them to basically compound on each other.
claims.claim: Open weights let Chinese labs build on, distill and remix each other's work, speeding progress without separate giant training clusters.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: There was a a release today of a quen you know 30 billion parameter model which is performing as good as GPT40.
claims.claim: Leading models are distilled to small, cheap models fast: a 30B-parameter Qwen matched GPT-4o performance.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: the Chinese just have been able to work around that because of, you know, their position on IP.
claims.claim: China's weaker IP and copyright stance lets its model makers train on copyrighted data freely, an advantage over US labs.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: this might allow them to pass the best proprietary models coming out of the US um yet this year, maybe by Q4 of this year.
claims.claim: Prediction that Chinese open-source models may pass the best US proprietary models by Q4 2025.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we've trained them to use tools like the internet, right? The they're true reasoning engines.
claims.claim: Models that use tools (web search) need not compress the whole internet, so reasoning models shift the open vs closed balance and cut the size and cost needed.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: and once they're coupled with strong tools you start getting these really really incredible results that don't even just show up in benchmarks
claims.claim: Reasoning models coupled with tools perform better than benchmarks show because benchmarks do not allow tool use.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: China got excited about open source about 20 years ago.
claims.claim: China's long embrace of open source (Linux) and weaker IP protection made open-weights AI a natural strategy.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: when you have a competitive dynamic where every single player, and I think there may be seven or eight deep pocketed players with open models in China, they they all learn from each other extremely fast.
claims.claim: Seven or eight well-funded Chinese open-model labs co-evolve fast through distillation, producing quick progress unlike software competition.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the community where the best practices are shared across all farms is going to have a higher global output for the community than the one where you've just got proprietary ideas
claims.claim: Shared best practices (open source) give a community higher output and less chance of a breakout monopolist than closed competition.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: had a section they did which which is about encouraging open-source and open weight models in the US
claims.claim: The US AI Action Plan (July 2025) encourages open-source/open-weight US models; China responded with a call for a global AI cooperation organization.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: is 90% of the quality in terms of intelligence, but at a 90% price discount.
claims.claim: Leading Chinese open models offer about 90% of frontier intelligence at about a 90% lower price, driving demand from developers and enterprises.
claims.indicator: intelligence vs price per million tokens

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: They want some accountability. And that's what you'll get. That's what you sort of got out of Linux and say Red Hat, right?
claims.claim: Enterprises want an accountable vendor for open-source software (Red Hat for Linux), so a US-domiciled open model company could win.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: I'd be willing to say, you know, the a top three worldwide model will be a US-based open source model.
claims.claim: Prediction: by Q4 2025 or Q1 2026 a top-three model worldwide will be a US-based open source model (OpenAI open model, Meta).

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: And so for any large tech company, commoditizing a a potential threat is is actually quite valuable.
claims.claim: Large tech firms that are not winning on offense fund open source to commoditize a rival (Facebook Open Compute; Alibaba funding Zhipu).

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: if I'm at any of those companies, I'd be funding a open-source competitor
claims.claim: Laggard big tech (Microsoft, Amazon, Apple) should fund open-source competitors instead of backing a proprietary lab.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: if you start with access to those Chinese models it wouldn't take you long to move into a near place and you wouldn't have to spend the kind of money the foundational model companies have.
claims.claim: New US entrants can start from Chinese open models and reach near-frontier quality without frontier-lab spending, and regulatory capture fights may follow.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: two things that we see is brand and you know the US doiciled or you know someone that they can kind of point at that wins
claims.claim: Enterprises pick a US-domiciled, liable provider when capability and price are equal, so a competitive US open model would win share back.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: My hunch is that they're going to stay very committed to open source, but they may complement it with a proprietary model.
claims.claim: Meta is likely to stay open-source while adding a proprietary model.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: So it turns out if you deliver something really powerful and really cheap that's more important to these players than American values aligned.
claims.claim: Global buyers choose cheap powerful models over values-aligned ones, but a model that is both would top the leaderboards.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the cycle time on the innovation in the open source community out of China. It's faster and better at the moment.
claims.claim: Chinese open-source release cadence and quality now exceeds the US open-source ecosystem.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: If you look at this one out of Elon talking about the X.AI AI goal is 50 million in units of H100 equivalent.
claims.claim: xAI's goal of 50 million H100-equivalents (about 4M GPUs, 11 GW) and OpenAI's 4.5 GW Abilene deal show planned compute is far larger than a year ago.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: So these compute clusters now that are being talked about being built over the next 5 years, these are massively bigger than what we were even talking about a year ago.
claims.claim: Inference-time reasoning and agent-to-agent interaction raise compute demand, refuting the earlier overbuild (Cisco 2000) concern.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: Google went from 5 trillion tokens a month to 480 trillion tokens a month.
claims.claim: Google's monthly tokens grew from 5T to 480T and then above 1 quadrillion, about 200x in a little over a year.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: anywhere we lay infrastructure um we fire up a rack it becomes fully consumed within a few hours.
claims.claim: Groq inference capacity is fully consumed within hours of deployment, so demand outstrips supply.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: In the case of Anthropic, it's, you know, uh 170 billion on rumored $5 billion in revenue.
claims.claim: AI lab funding rounds (Anthropic about $170B on about $5B revenue, xAI $150-200B) are unprecedented in venture history, with option dilution debated.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: for the first time ever you saw private companies have a competitive advantage and that they can be more risk-seeking with capital than the public companies are allowed to be.
claims.claim: Private labs can lose money (OpenAI about $7B a year) that public companies like Google would not allow, a new competitive advantage.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: the cost is no object the CNO group
claims.claim: OpenAI, Meta and X form a cost-is-no-object spending group while Microsoft and Amazon hold back capex, leaving a split in AI investment intensity.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: they're the winners um in a pick and shovel game that's got this amount of aggressiveness.
claims.claim: Nvidia, Dell and possibly SK Hynix are the winners of AI capex as suppliers.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: 10 to 100x more than the your very first AI search.
claims.claim: Reasoning models consume 10-100x more tokens per query, a driver of token growth.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: Anthropic had to put this uh you know, press release plus, you know, product change out saying
claims.claim: Anthropic throttling users shows demand exceeds supply and no evidence yet of oversupply.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: And so everyone's pricing to share. That means they're pricing under cost.
claims.claim: AI model companies price below cost for market share, with rumors of negative gross margin, so a repricing would create a bump in supply and demand when it ends.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: like the thing that throttles demand is price, but no one here is raising price.
claims.claim: Compute scarcity could be solved by raising price, but vendors fear losing share, so shortage is partly artificial.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the steepness of that price curve on you know as you as it kind of becomes you know less less cutting edge is something I've never seen before.
claims.claim: Prices fall very steeply for older model generations, so users can switch to older or cheaper models to cut losses.
claims.indicator: price per token by model age

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: in the internet age all the startups began with Oracle and Sun and eventually they all moved to Linux and MySQL.
claims.claim: Analogy: startups first win at all cost, then optimize cost with open source; AI inference users are starting to optimize cost now.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: multiple folks are building their own models uh based off open source
claims.claim: Coding-agent companies can distill open models under Apache licenses to replace expensive proprietary APIs for most use cases.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Amazon had this monopoly retail business they could use to subsidize AWS gain share for a decade and then begin to take price.
claims.claim: OpenAI can use its high-margin consumer business to subsidize a cheap open model for price-sensitive coding workloads, as Amazon did with AWS.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: they all exist at the beneficence of the capital markets and the capital markets are willing to provide an incredible amount of capital to these businesses today.
claims.claim: Share-seeking labs depend on capital markets and funding can disappear quickly, so labs without consumer products are vulnerable.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: how many non-G Google uh applications are running on the TPUs like how many third party customers are using
claims.claim: Google's TPU advantage depends on third-party use, as most TPU volume is internal.

claims.speaker: Bill Gurley
claims.quote: OpenAI's um most likely chance to long-term um success comes from switching cost and lock in more than it will come from staying on the edge of the of the model race
claims.claim: User memory and history create switching costs and pricing power for ChatGPT even if models commoditize.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the battle for the consumer is ultimately where the value occurs, Sunny, not who runs, you know, what hardware.
claims.claim: Value accrues to whoever owns the consumer (as Google search did for 20 years), and ChatGPT is the first real threat.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the model layer is being increasingly commoditized and that there's not going to be a lot of intrinsic value in in in that intelligence layer
claims.claim: Open-source distillation drives intelligence up and cost down, so model value shifts to applications.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think chat GBT will cross a billion weeklys like maybe this year.
claims.claim: ChatGPT may exceed one billion weekly users in 2025.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think they're going to be lots of players that compete. I think the margins will be lower.
claims.claim: AI will be a heterogeneous market with many competitors and lower margins, yet a rising tide lets many do well; OpenAI plus Anthropic are worth over $500B.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: We all voted with our wallets and we said until the president tells us whether it's door one or door two, we're out.
claims.claim: Markets sold off on Liberation Day because tariff outcomes ranged from about $300B (Bessent/Lutnick) to $2T (Navarro) and risk was unpriceable.
claims.direction: exit equities when policy range is wide

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: The NASDAQ was down 21% right at its trough this year.
claims.claim: The Nasdaq fell 21% at the April trough then rose over 30% in 60-70 days once the lower tariff path became clear.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think the consensus view of all economists, right, 90% of economists is that tariffs are going to be bad.
claims.claim: Consensus (about 90% of economists) expected tariffs to be a tax paid by US consumers and cause inflation.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: if we impose a 15% tariff on them they have to eat it the producers have to eat it because otherwise they're going end up laying off millions of people
claims.claim: Bessent/Hassett theory: because exporters depend on the US market (deficit about $1.2T in goods), modest tariffs are absorbed by foreign producers.
claims.testable: yes - import price pass-through can be measured

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: Import prices have been going up at a slower rate than domestically produced goods.
claims.claim: NEC analysis of core PCE shows import prices rising slower than domestic goods, with no pass-through of tariffs yet, though inflation could still come.
claims.indicator: core PCE; import prices vs domestic goods prices

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: and the fact that we now have a 300 to a $350 billion recurring, you know, stream of revenues into Treasury in the form of these tariffs which are being paid.
claims.claim: Tariffs create about $300-350B a year in Treasury revenue, relevant to deficits.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the month of June we had our first surplus in the United States monthly surplus since 2015 right because of the tariff revenues that are coming in.
claims.claim: June 2025 produced the first monthly US budget surplus since 2015 due to tariff revenue.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: core PCE h did bottom last year and it started to tick up and so we have to keep our eye on inflation.
claims.claim: Core PCE bottomed in 2024 and is rising, so tariff pass-through risk requires monitoring.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the Atlanta now Fed tracker which tracks real-time GDP has now ticked up back to 3%.
claims.claim: The Atlanta Fed GDPNow rebounded to 3% after April's drop, supporting the view tariffs did not hurt activity.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: The voting machine is telling you that no retaliations, no trade wars, all these deals getting done um uh works for the US economy.
claims.claim: Market prices are a better read of tariff policy than economist warnings (Summers called it a disaster).

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: these are now viable investments because of the tariffs and the resolve of the government to reonshore these critical supply chains.
claims.claim: Tariffs make US onshoring (rare earth magnets, chips, data centers, energy) investable.

claims.speaker: Sunny Madra
claims.quote: we've seen you know our tariff schedule move around probably six to eight times since this all has started
claims.claim: The administration revised the tariff schedule six to eight times after supplier feedback, making policy adaptive and uncertainty decay.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think this president wants to do the biggest deal ever done with China.
claims.claim: View that a large US-China deal (rare earths, chips, trade rebalancing) is coming and consensus underestimates it.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: we do, I think, $900 billion of trade with them a year. With China, it's about 600 billion, but we have about a $300 billion goods trade deficit with both Europe and China.
claims.claim: The EU and China each represent a roughly $300B US goods deficit, so they were the key targets.
claims.indicator: US goods trade deficit by partner

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: the rare earth ban on Chinese magnets was devastating to US industry.
claims.claim: China's rare earth ban and the US H20 chip cutoff show retaliation channels that create supply-chain risk.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I don't think we're going below 15%.
claims.claim: Expected US tariff on China floor of 15% (the pre-Trump rate plus), with a more structured deal.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I think that there's going to be a big Chinese deal done before the year's out.
claims.claim: China must rebalance toward domestic consumption over years, and a large US-China deal before year-end would lift markets.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: On May 2nd, I said we're all we're all back in because the Bessant consensus has won.
claims.claim: Altimeter went out of equities in March and back in May 2nd once the Bessent 300B tariff path won, getting the Nasdaq rebound.

claims.speaker: Brad Gerstner
claims.quote: I would have said the market can be up at least 15% for the year I think we've captured a lot of the return for the for the year
claims.claim: With S&P and Nasdaq up about 10% YTD and a 15% year target, much of the 2025 return was already captured, though AI opportunities remain.
